questions.stem: How does microevolution differ from macroevolution?
options: Microevolution changes allele frequencies in a population; macroevolution is change above species level
Microevolution happens only in microorganisms; macroevolution happens only in large animals and plants
Microevolution is change above species level; macroevolution changes allele frequencies in a population
Microevolution is caused by mutation alone; macroevolution is caused by natural selection alone
questions.explanation: Microevolution is small-scale change in the allele frequencies of a population's gene pool over generations. Macroevolution is large-scale change, such as the origin of new species and higher groups, which results from microevolutionary changes accumulating over long periods.

questions.stem: Over 30 years, the frequency of an insecticide-resistance allele in a mosquito population rises from 0.05 to 0.60 where the insecticide is sprayed. This is best described as:
options: microevolution, driven by natural selection
macroevolution, driven by natural selection
microevolution, driven by gene flow alone
macroevolution, driven by genetic drift
questions.explanation: A change in allele frequency within one population is microevolution. The insecticide is a selection pressure: resistant mosquitoes survive and reproduce more, so the allele becomes more common. No new species has formed, so it is not macroevolution.

questions.stem: Why does mutation on its own usually change allele frequencies in a population only very slowly?
options: Mutations happen only when the environment is changing rapidly
Each new mutation is rare and first appears in a single individual
Mutations occur only in body cells and so are never inherited
Mutations always produce harmful alleles that are lost at once
questions.explanation: Mutation is the source of new alleles, but any particular mutation arises rarely and begins in one individual. Large changes in frequency need selection or drift acting on it. Mutations in gametes or the cells that make them are inherited, and many mutations are neutral.

questions.stem: What is the effect of ongoing gene flow between two populations of the same species?
options: Their gene pools become more different from each other
Each population loses every allele it shared with the other
Both populations stop producing any new mutations at all
Their gene pools become more similar to each other
questions.explanation: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding. It mixes the gene pools and works against the populations diverging, which is why reduced gene flow is needed for speciation.

questions.stem: In which population is genetic drift likely to change allele frequencies the most?
options: A population of 5000 kept stable by selection
A population of 2000 with constant gene flow
An isolated population of 20 rock-wallabies
A connected population of 20 000 rock-wallabies
questions.explanation: Drift is random change in allele frequency, and chance events have the largest proportional effect in small populations. A small, isolated population also receives no new alleles by gene flow to offset losses.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions is needed for natural selection to occur?
options: Heritable variation, more offspring than can survive, and differences in survival and reproduction
Identical individuals, unlimited resources, and equal survival and reproduction of all offspring
Heritable variation, unlimited resources, and equal survival and reproduction of all offspring
Identical individuals, more offspring than can survive, and survival decided by chance alone
questions.explanation: Natural selection needs variation that is inherited, a struggle for survival because more offspring are produced than resources can support, and individuals with some variants surviving and reproducing more than others. Without heritable variation or differential survival, allele frequencies cannot change by selection.

questions.stem: Historically, babies of very low or very high birth weight had higher death rates than babies of medium birth weight. What type of selection does this show?
options: Sexual selection
Stabilising selection
Directional selection
Disruptive selection
questions.explanation: Selection against both extremes favours the intermediate phenotype, which is stabilising selection. It keeps the mean the same and narrows the range. Directional selection favours one extreme, and disruptive selection favours both extremes.

questions.stem: After a severe drought on a Galapagos island, mostly large, hard seeds remained, and ground finches with deeper beaks survived better. In later generations average beak depth increased. What type of selection is this?
options: Disruptive selection
Genetic drift
Directional selection
Stabilising selection
questions.explanation: Selection favoured one extreme of the range, deeper beaks, so the mean shifted in that direction: directional selection. The survival difference was linked to beak depth, so the change was not random drift.

questions.stem: In a seed-eating bird, individuals with small bills feed well on soft seeds and those with large bills on hard seeds, but birds with medium bills feed poorly on both. What change in the distribution of bill size is expected over generations?
options: The single peak shifts towards larger bills, and small bills are lost
The distribution stays the same, as all three sizes keep surviving
Two peaks form at small and large sizes, with fewer medium bills
One peak forms at medium size, with fewer small and large bills
questions.explanation: Selection against the intermediate phenotype while both extremes are favoured is disruptive selection, giving a bimodal distribution with two peaks. Favouring the middle would be stabilising selection, and favouring one extreme directional selection.

questions.stem: Graphs of a trait in a population before and after many generations of selection show that afterwards the mean is the same but the spread of values is much narrower. Which type of selection is shown?
options: Disruptive selection
Gene flow
Stabilising selection
Directional selection
questions.explanation: An unchanged mean with reduced variation means individuals at both extremes were selected against, which is stabilising selection. Directional selection would shift the mean, and disruptive selection would widen the spread or split it into two peaks.

questions.stem: A beetle population of 500 contains 245 BB, 210 Bb and 45 bb individuals. What is the frequency of allele B?
questions.explanation: There are 1000 alleles in 500 diploid beetles. Allele B is carried twice by each BB beetle and once by each Bb beetle: (2 × 245) + 210 = 700, and 700/1000 = 0.70. The value 0.49 is the proportion of BB individuals, not the allele frequency.

questions.stem: Flower colour shows incomplete dominance: RR plants are red, RW pink and WW white. A population of 400 plants has 64 red, 192 pink and 144 white. What is the frequency of allele R?
questions.explanation: The 400 plants carry 800 alleles. R alleles = (2 × 64) + 192 = 320, and 320/800 = 0.40. The value 0.16 is the proportion of red plants, and 0.60 is the frequency of allele W.

questions.stem: After a predator that easily sees dd fish is introduced, the frequency of allele d in a fish population is 0.50, 0.38, 0.24 and 0.12 at generations 0, 5, 10 and 15. Which statement is best supported?
options: The change is genetic drift, because it is steady rather than sudden
Allele d is under negative selection, because the predator removes dd fish
Allele d is under positive selection, because its frequency changes steadily
Allele D is under negative selection, because its frequency is falling
questions.explanation: The predator removes fish showing the dd phenotype, so allele d is selected against and falls steadily: negative selection. Allele D rises from 0.50 to 0.88, so it is under positive selection. A steady, consistent trend linked to a selection pressure is not random drift.

questions.stem: In hospital bacteria exposed to an antibiotic, the frequency of a resistance allele rose from 0.02 to 0.90 over several years. In bacteria in the community, where the antibiotic was rarely used, it stayed near 0.02. Which explanation fits?
options: The antibiotic selected for the existing resistance allele where it was used
The antibiotic caused the resistance mutation to arise in hospital bacteria
Gene flow from community bacteria raised the allele frequency in hospitals
Genetic drift raised the allele frequency only in the hospital bacteria
questions.explanation: The rise happened only where the selection pressure was present, so positive selection best explains it: resistant bacteria survived and reproduced while others died. The antibiotic did not cause the mutation, and community bacteria had a low frequency, so gene flow from them could not raise it to 0.90.

questions.stem: Which is an example of divergent evolution?
options: A flowering plant and its pollinator each evolving in response to the other
Two related lineages independently evolving the same trait in similar habitats
Related species from one ancestor evolving different beaks for different foods
Unrelated sharks and dolphins both evolving streamlined bodies for fast swimming
questions.explanation: Divergent evolution occurs when descendants of a common ancestor become increasingly different as they adapt to different environments or niches. Similar bodies in unrelated animals are convergent evolution, and plants and pollinators changing in response to each other is coevolution.

questions.stem: Sharks, which are fish, and dolphins, which are mammals, both have streamlined bodies and fins. Which pattern of evolution does this show?
options: Divergent evolution
Parallel evolution
Coevolution
Convergent evolution
questions.explanation: Sharks and dolphins are distantly related, but similar selection pressures in water produced similar body shapes independently, which is convergent evolution. Their similarities are analogous, not inherited from a shared streamlined ancestor.

questions.stem: Two closely related lizard species, descended from a recent common ancestor, live on separate islands with similar habitats. Starting from the same short-legged ancestral form, each independently evolves long legs. Which pattern of evolution is this?
options: Parallel evolution
Convergent evolution
Divergent evolution
Coevolution
questions.explanation: Parallel evolution is when related lineages, starting from a similar ancestral condition, independently evolve similar traits under similar pressures. Convergent evolution produces similar traits in distantly related lineages that started from different forms.

questions.stem: Darwin examined an orchid from Madagascar with a very long nectar spur and predicted it must be pollinated by a moth with an equally long tongue. Such a moth was later discovered. Which process explains the match?
options: Coevolution, with each species acting as a selection pressure on the other
Convergent evolution, with the two species starting from different ancestors
Divergent evolution, with the two species splitting from a common ancestor
Genetic drift, with both species changing randomly over the same period
questions.explanation: Longer spurs favoured moths with longer tongues, and longer-tongued moths favoured flowers with longer spurs, so each species drove change in the other: coevolution. The moth and the orchid are not related lineages producing similar features, so neither convergent nor divergent evolution applies.

questions.stem: Which type of isolation leads to allopatric speciation?
options: Geographic isolation by a physical barrier
Temporal isolation within the same area
Behavioural isolation within one population
Partial isolation along a shared boundary
questions.explanation: In allopatric speciation a population is split by a geographic barrier such as a sea, river or mountain range, which stops gene flow so the populations diverge. Speciation without a geographic barrier in the same area is sympatric, and between adjacent populations along a boundary is parapatric.

questions.stem: Some apple maggot flies in North America lay their eggs on apples, which ripen earlier than hawthorn fruit, their original host. Flies mate on their host fruit, so the two groups breed at different times in the same area. What could this lead to?
options: Allopatric speciation, through geographic isolation
Parapatric speciation, along an abrupt boundary
Convergent evolution of the two separate groups
Sympatric speciation, through temporal isolation
questions.explanation: The two groups live in the same area, but breeding at different times on different hosts reduces gene flow between them. Divergence without a geographic barrier is sympatric speciation, and differences in breeding time are temporal isolation.

questions.stem: A grass population spreads from a pasture onto neighbouring mine waste rich in heavy metals. Plants on the waste become metal-tolerant and flower at a slightly different time, so gene flow across the boundary is reduced. Which type of speciation could this lead to?
options: Allopatric speciation
Sympatric speciation
Coevolution
Parapatric speciation
questions.explanation: The two populations are adjacent along an environmental boundary, with some contact but reduced gene flow, and they experience different selection pressures. Divergence of neighbouring populations in this way is parapatric speciation. There is no geographic barrier separating them, so it is not allopatric.

questions.stem: Why must gene flow between two populations be reduced or stopped before they can become separate species?
options: Natural selection can act only in populations that have no gene flow
Alleles moving between the populations keep their gene pools similar
Gene flow causes harmful mutations that kill any hybrid offspring
Gene flow increases genetic drift until both populations die out
questions.explanation: While populations interbreed, gene flow spreads alleles between them and counters the divergence caused by selection, drift and mutation. Once gene flow is reduced, the gene pools can change independently until reproductive isolation develops.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes allopatric speciation?
options: A barrier splits a population; reproductive isolation develops; gene flow stops; the groups diverge
A barrier splits a population; gene flow stops; the groups diverge; reproductive isolation develops
The groups diverge; a barrier splits the population; reproductive isolation develops; gene flow stops
Reproductive isolation develops; a barrier splits a population; gene flow stops; the groups diverge
questions.explanation: A geographic barrier first divides the population and stops gene flow. Different selection pressures, mutation and drift then change each gene pool independently, until the populations can no longer interbreed even if the barrier is removed. Reproductive isolation is the outcome of divergence, not its starting point.

questions.stem: A small, isolated possum population has become inbred and has very low genetic diversity. Why does it face a higher risk of extinction, even if its habitat is protected?
options: Inbreeding causes the possums to stop competing for food with other species
Few alleles limit adaptation to change, and harmful recessive alleles are expressed more
Inbred populations always produce more offspring, so they exceed the carrying capacity
Low diversity stops all new mutations from occurring in the population's gametes
questions.explanation: With few alleles, the population may lack variants that could survive a new disease or a change in climate. Inbreeding also raises homozygosity, so harmful recessive alleles are expressed more often, lowering survival and fertility.

questions.stem: What is comparative genomics?
options: Comparing the DNA profiles of suspects with samples from a crime scene
Comparing the genome sequences of different species to find similarities and differences
Comparing the external body features and behaviour of different species to classify them
Comparing the karyotypes of individuals to detect chromosomal abnormalities
questions.explanation: Comparative genomics compares DNA sequences, genes and genome organisation across species. Shared sequences and the number of differences between them provide evidence for common ancestry and how closely species are related.

questions.stem: Comparative genomics shows that humans and mice share thousands of genes with very similar sequences, often in a similar order on their chromosomes. What is the best explanation?
options: Genes with similar roles always evolve identical sequences anew
Both species inherited these genes from a shared common ancestor
Similar environments caused the same mutations in both species
Gene flow between mice and humans transferred the genes directly
questions.explanation: Shared sequences, and shared gene order, are best explained by inheritance from a common ancestor, with differences accumulating since the lineages split. Environments do not cause particular mutations, and gene flow occurs only between interbreeding populations of the same species.

questions.stem: Why are highly conserved sequences, such as ribosomal RNA genes, useful for comparing very distantly related organisms?
options: They change quickly, so even close relatives show many differences in these genes
They are found only in animals, so they are easy to compare across animal groups
They do not code for anything, so they are never affected by natural selection
They change slowly because most mutations in them are harmful, so similarities persist
questions.explanation: Conserved sequences carry out essential functions, so most mutations in them are removed by selection and they change slowly. Similarities therefore remain detectable even between organisms that diverged a very long time ago. Ribosomal RNA genes are found in all living things.

questions.stem: Fossils show species A and B diverged 10 million years ago, and a conserved gene differs between them at 8 positions. The same gene differs between A and C at 20 positions. Assuming a constant rate of change, when did A and C diverge?
options: About 12.5 million years ago
About 4 million years ago
About 200 million years ago
About 25 million years ago
questions.explanation: The calibration is 8 differences per 10 million years, so 20 differences correspond to 20/8 × 10 = 25 million years. This use of conserved sequences as a molecular clock depends on the rate of change being roughly constant. The value 4 million years comes from inverting the ratio.

questions.stem: In a phylogram, what do the branch lengths represent?
options: The number of species living in each lineage
The body size of the organisms in each lineage
Nothing; only the order of branching matters
The amount of genetic change along each lineage
questions.explanation: A phylogram is drawn so that branch lengths are proportional to the amount of change, such as the number of base substitutions. In a cladogram, branch lengths have no meaning, and only the order of branching shows relatedness.

questions.stem: A cladogram shows species D branching off first, then species C, and finally species A and B splitting from each other. Which statement is correct?
options: A and B share the most recent common ancestor of any pair
D is the ancestor from which species A, B and C evolved
C is more closely related to D than it is to A or B
A is more closely related to C than it is to B
questions.explanation: The last split on the tree is between A and B, so they share the most recent common ancestor. D is not an ancestor; it is a living species that branched off earliest. C shares a more recent ancestor with A and B than with D.

questions.stem: On the same cladogram, D branches first, then C, then A and B split. A student says C is more closely related to B than to A because C is drawn beside B. What is the correct relationship?
options: C is equally related to A and B, sharing one common ancestor with both
C is more closely related to B, because the two are drawn side by side
C is more closely related to A, because A is listed first on the tree
C is more closely related to D, because C and D branched off earliest
questions.explanation: A and B both descend from the node where they split, and C joins them at the same earlier node, so C is equally related to A and B. The order in which tips are drawn can be rotated at any node without changing the relationships.

questions.stem: For a 20-base section of a gene, species P and Q differ at 2 positions, P and R at 9 positions, and Q and R at 8 positions. Which relationship is best supported?
options: P and R share the most recent common ancestor, with Q more distant
Q and R share the most recent common ancestor, with P more distant
All three species are equally related, as each pair differs somewhat
P and Q share the most recent common ancestor, with R more distant
questions.explanation: Fewer sequence differences indicate a more recent common ancestor. P and Q differ at only 2 positions, far fewer than either differs from R, so they are each other's closest relatives on the tree.

questions.stem: In a phylogram, two sister species X and Y branch from the same node, but the branch leading to X is much longer than the branch leading to Y. What does this show?
options: X diverged from the common ancestor much earlier than Y diverged from it
X is the ancestor of Y, so X must have existed for a longer time
X is less closely related to Y than Y is to X on this phylogram
X's lineage has accumulated more genetic change since the two diverged
questions.explanation: Sister species diverged at the same moment, at their shared node. In a phylogram branch length shows the amount of change, so the longer branch means X's lineage changed more, for example through a faster mutation rate. Relatedness is symmetrical, so X cannot be less closely related to Y than Y is to X.

questions.stem: According to the fossil record, life on Earth has a history of approximately how long?
options: 540 million years
66 million years
350 million years
3.5 billion years
questions.explanation: The oldest widely accepted fossil evidence of life, from microbial structures, is about 3.5 billion years old. About 540 million years ago marks the rapid appearance of many animal groups, and 66 million years ago the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs.

questions.stem: Which is generally recognised as the largest mass extinction in the history of life?
options: The end-Triassic extinction, about 201 million years ago
The end-Permian extinction, about 252 million years ago
The end-Cretaceous extinction, about 66 million years ago
The end-Ordovician extinction, about 444 million years ago
questions.explanation: The end-Permian extinction wiped out the greatest proportion of marine and land species of any mass extinction. The end-Cretaceous extinction, which ended the non-avian dinosaurs, is the best known but was smaller.

questions.stem: After the non-avian dinosaurs became extinct about 66 million years ago, mammals diversified into many new forms. What is this an example of?
options: A mass extinction caused by competition
Convergent evolution from many ancestors
Stabilising selection on a single species
An evolutionary radiation into vacant niches
questions.explanation: The extinction left many niches empty, and surviving mammal lineages diversified rapidly to fill them, an adaptive or evolutionary radiation. Radiation produces many species from relatively few ancestors, which is divergent, not convergent.

questions.stem: A timescale graph shows the number of marine animal families rising, then falling sharply around 252 million years ago, then rising rapidly over the following tens of millions of years. How should this be interpreted?
options: A gap in the fossil record, as no rocks formed during this time
A mass extinction, followed by an evolutionary radiation of survivors
An evolutionary radiation, followed by a mass extinction of survivors
A period of stabilising selection that slowly reduced the families
questions.explanation: A sharp fall in the number of families marks a mass extinction, here the end-Permian. The rapid rise afterwards shows surviving lineages diversifying to fill vacated niches, an evolutionary radiation. A slow, selection-driven decline would not show such a sudden drop.

questions.stem: About 540 million years ago, most major animal groups appear in the fossil record within a relatively short time. What is this event an example of?
options: A mass extinction
Convergent evolution
A population bottleneck
An evolutionary radiation
questions.explanation: The rapid appearance of many animal phyla at the start of the Cambrian, often called the Cambrian explosion, is an evolutionary radiation. A mass extinction is a sudden loss, not a gain, of many groups.
